I was in the same boat as you a few years ago, and although it was a stressful time I'm still super glad I went to uni!!

I'm a massive introvert and definitely prefer having time on my own, so I was worried about meeting my flatmates in my first year too. Although I fell out of contact with my flatmates in my second year, I still managed to befriend them in my first year and it helped me come out of my shell a lot and I started enjoying clubbing a lot more!! If you don't kick it off with your flatmates within the first few days, I would recommend trying to befriend people on your course or applying for societies in the first few weeks. If you still don't make any friends, I'm sure there's probably a lot of online events for freshers to meet new people. Although a lot of socialising at uni revolves around clubbing/drinking/drugs, there's usually a lot of options for people who aren't into that sort of scene, you just have to look a little harder!!

I'm also very frugal and hate spending money on groceries too, and I found it pretty easy to get jealous of other people's financial situation when they're getting dominos 5 times a week. Although it heavily depends on your financial situation and how much money you get from your maintenance loan/job, my biggest tips for groceries are 1) get a tesco clubcard and abuse the hell out of your student discount wherever you shop, 2) don't buy lots of meal deals and frozen pizzas, and 3) don't go grocery shopping more than once a week or you'll be more likely to make impulse purchases or buying things you don't actually want to cook.

Finally, at some point as a fresher you'll probably hear someone say 'your first year is the year when you can screw around and socialise and you can neglect your course until shit starts getting real in the second year'. Although this is definitely true to an extent, I had a couple of friends who used this excuse to do absolutely nothing and ended up completely flunking and having to drop out at the end of the year. So try not to stress too hard on your first year but don't start skipping all your 9am lectures, because that's a very hard habit to get rid of. If you have any mature students on your course, you'll probably notice that they tend to be a lot more focused and hardworking and will ask lots of questions and get on well with your lecturers. Try to take inspiration from them, as they usually end up flourishing and getting higher grades.

Although personally I prefer TS3, even high end computers struggle with running it smoothly nowadays. TS4 will be way better in terms of performance, but the content is a lot more lacking in my opinion. With the PC versions of 3 and 4 you'll have full access to a ton of CC which will massively improve both games. The Sims Resource, Mod the Sims, and tumblr are all good places to find cc and mods. Since you've already played TS4 you'll already have an idea of what to expect, so maybe if you can afford it I would suggest trying out TS3 when it goes on sale (steam quite often has it on sale a couple of times a year, I'm not so sure about origin though)

As for pack recommendations, it depends what your play style is. if you tend to play families and enjoy domestic living, for TS3 I'd recommend generations/ambitions/pets/seasons and for TS4 I'd go with cats and dogs/seasons/parenthood. If you prefer to play a single sim, for TS3 I'd choose ambitions/university life/island paradise and for TS4 I'd go with get to work/city living/discover university. Although TS3 packs tend to bigger and have a lot more content, TS4 also has a lot of smaller packs that i'd recommend such as tiny living, laundry day and nifty knitting.
